items.title: Nvidia RTX Spark laptops running Linux experience GPU clock speed throttling to 780 MHz due to encrypted power management firmware, reducing inference speed to 35% of Windows performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
items.summary:
Linux can be installed and run on Nvidia RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus with GPU acceleration via Nvidia's open kernel driver, but the GPU clock speed is limited to about 780 MHz when plugged in, compared to over 2 GHz on Windows. This slowdown is caused by a Windows-only power management component called Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework, which manages power delivery and decrypts firmware power tables that Linux cannot access. As a result, inference speed on Linux drops to roughly 14 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model, compared to 65 tokens per second on Windows.

Installing Linux requires workarounds for hardware support and memory allocation, as the laptop reserves a large portion of unified memory for the GPU by default, adjustable only from Windows. Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) offers a practical alternative by running Linux tools on top of the Windows driver stack, maintaining full GPU performance. A full Linux fix depends on Nvidia porting the platform controller's power management logic to its Linux driver, which would enable the laptop to perform comparably to Nvidia's DGX Spark desktop system.

items.title: Report: Postman desktop auto-installs Codex and Claude AI plugins, modifies user coding agents and attempts to approve its own startup hook without explicit consent [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
items.summary:
Users reported that opening Postman on Mac triggered automatic installation of Codex and Claude AI plugins, altered global user configurations, and routed API tasks through Postman skills without explicit permission. The installation also included a Postman CLI and attempted to approve its own instruction hook, raising concerns about consent and trust boundaries.

Investigation found logs confirming the automatic plugin installation and configuration changes that directed broad API work into Postman. The installer enabled a remote MCP connection without proper authentication and modified multiple coding agents, which users consider a severe breach of expected behavior for an API client.

This behavior has sparked discussions about user consent and security implications, as the automatic changes affect unrelated tools and workflows. The report does not confirm data exfiltration but highlights significant integration and instruction modifications made silently by Postman.

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B running on a laptop can interpret and analyze raw neural network weights, replicating capabilities shown by GPT-6 Astra in recent research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.summary:
A recent paper demonstrated that GPT-6 Astra can interpret and modify raw neural network weights to improve model performance without training loops, a process termed Weight-Space Programming. Simon Willison tested this approach with Qwen 3.8 27B on his laptop and found it could similarly analyze model weights and identify training tasks.

The research involved feeding floating point weight data from networks trained to play classic games into large language models, which then inferred the game each network was trained on. This capability extends to identifying and correcting issues in model weights to enhance performance, as shown by GPT-6 Astra's improvements on math reasoning tasks. Willison's experiments with Qwen 3.8 27B confirm that such weight-space interpretation is possible on smaller models without external tools or code execution.

items.originalTitle: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
items.summary: This book provides a concise, derivation-focused overview of the mathematical foundations underlying modern generative AI models. It connects major families of generative models such as PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, normalizing flows, autoregressive models, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models, aiming to clarify their structure and relationships without sacrificing mathematical depth. The primer is designed for researchers, practitioners, and students interested in a foundational understanding of generative modeling techniques.

items.title: Geoffrey Hinton warns AI risks could trigger major incidents like power or financial system shutdowns and suggests humanity might have been better off without AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
items.summary:
Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer of artificial intelligence and Nobel laureate, expressed concerns that AI development might ultimately harm society, potentially causing large-scale disruptions such as blackouts or financial system failures. While he acknowledges AI's potential for a positive future, he warns that failure to manage its risks could lead to severe social and economic problems.

Hinton criticized leaders of major AI companies for prioritizing profit over safety and called for stricter regulation akin to drug approval processes to ensure AI models do more good than harm. He highlighted the urgency of global cooperation on AI standards and testing, contrasting this with current self-regulation approaches favored by some political figures. Hinton's remarks come amid growing debate over AI governance and the potential consequences of unchecked AI advancement.

items.originalTitle: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
items.summary: Users of Google's Gemini chatbot have reported that their chat histories, including those from paid subscribers, are used to train AI models unless they disable the 'Keep Activity' setting. Google’s support documentation confirms that chats may be reviewed by human reviewers and retained for up to three years, even if users delete their activity. To prevent training on their conversations, users must turn off this setting, which also deletes chat sessions after 72 hours, a detail some users only discovered after subscribing.

The engineer emphasizes the transformative impact of AI agents on software development, enabling rapid prototyping, bug fixing, and experimentation while noting the ongoing need for human oversight to maintain quality. They also discuss the cognitive challenges of managing multiple AI agents simultaneously and the broader implications of AI integration into creative and professional tasks.

items.title: OpenAthena.ai says there is no posttraining data commons for AI, contrasting with abundant pretraining data from public internet archives [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: There is no posttraining data commons
items.summary: OpenAthena.ai argues that while large language models benefited from vast, freely available pretraining data sourced from public internet archives like Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and Project Gutenberg, there is no equivalent commons for posttraining data. Posttraining, which involves reinforcement learning on tasks rather than documents, requires durable, repeatable task data that does not naturally exist as a shared resource. The article highlights that human tasks are ephemeral and context-dependent, unlike the static documents used for pretraining, making the creation of a posttraining data commons challenging. It notes that software engineering is a notable exception where tasks are documented and preserved, which partly explains why agentic AI development has focused on software environments first.

items.title: Glow Labs finds AI coding agents installing deprecated MCP servers with known high-severity vulnerabilities from training data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI coding agents are installing abandoned MCP servers with known security issues
items.summary:
Glow Labs research identified a pattern where AI coding agents install deprecated Minecraft server software (MCP) that contains unpatched security vulnerabilities. These agents select outdated servers based on their training data rather than current, secure versions, exposing developer environments to risks. The deprecated servers, originally created by Anthropic, are widely used but no longer maintained or updated for security.

The research showed that in 98% of cases, agents chose deprecated MCP servers because they appeared in the training data, not because users requested them explicitly. This issue spans multiple AI tools and model providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI. The deprecated servers have millions of npm downloads but contain critical vulnerabilities such as remote code execution flaws, with maintainers confirming no future fixes. This raises concerns about automated code deployment relying on outdated packages without adequate vetting or awareness of deprecation notices.

items.title: Apple opens Siri AI integration to all developers with iOS 27.3 and related OS betas, enabling app intents and new voice capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Siri AI is now open to all developers
items.summary:
Apple has launched a Developer Preview allowing all developers to integrate their apps with the new Siri AI starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas. This update introduces deeper Siri AI capabilities including personal context understanding, natural language processing, and the ability to combine multiple actions into single experiences through skills, expanding Siri's functionality across Apple's ecosystem.

The new Siri AI supports multiple languages and is integrated into many Apple apps such as Calendar, Mail, Maps, and Messages, enabling users to perform complex tasks via voice commands. Developers can now use App Intents to bring their app content and actions directly into Siri AI, with plans to open App Store submissions in spring 2027. Apple is also working on usage policies and expanded access options for these AI features, which currently have daily limits and are unavailable in some regions like the EU.

items.title: Researchers explain why king minus man plus woman does not directly equal queen in word embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why king – man + woman isn't queen
items.summary:
The article explores the limitations of word embeddings in natural language processing, focusing on the common example where the vector arithmetic king - man + woman does not precisely yield queen. It highlights that embeddings capture general semantic directions rather than exact concept transformations, so subtracting man from king does not fully remove the male aspect, resulting in the nearest vector often being woman rather than queen.

The discussion includes experiments with small vocabularies and notes that excluding input words from candidate results can affect outcomes, as seen in original word2vec demonstrations. The article emphasizes that embeddings represent a lossy summary of meaning dominated by topic, and arithmetic moves vectors in a direction without teleporting to a specific concept, illustrating the complexities of linguistic structures and gendered titles in embedding spaces.

items.summary:
Umbra is an AI agent designed to run on Android devices that can operate apps autonomously in the background, allowing users to multitask without interruption. It reads screens, taps, types, scrolls, and manages apps while maintaining user control over risky actions such as payments or data deletion. The agent also includes a Linux environment for coding and testing software directly on the device, with persistent sessions that can pause and resume tasks even after crashes or restarts.

The system emphasizes user control and security by requiring approval for sensitive operations and maintaining detailed histories of agent actions. It supports multiple AI models and offers features like session file management, personal assistant agents, and automatic updates. Umbra is distributed as free software under the MIT License and is available via sideloading rather than through the Play Store.

items.title: Prime Intellect audits public LLM evaluations, identifies issues in AutomationBench and OfficeQA Pro v2, and releases fixes to improve benchmark accuracy and robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learnings from Auditing Public Evaluations
items.summary:
Prime Intellect analyzed popular public evaluations used for large language model (LLM) training, focusing on AutomationBench and OfficeQA Pro v2 benchmarks. They found problems such as unclear API request descriptions and overly strict grading scripts that affected model performance scores and interpretation. The team applied fixes including replacing prose request bodies with JSON Schemas and relaxing grading criteria, which significantly changed model scores and revealed some benchmarks are nearing saturation.

The audit included rewording tasks, adjusting grader requirements, and adding a mode to better simulate real-world tool usage, resulting in improved evaluation accuracy. Prime Intellect open-sourced these fixes to help the community enhance the reliability of public LLM benchmarks and recommended moving to updated benchmark versions for more meaningful assessments.

items.title: Fujifilm plans to increase magnetic tape production fivefold by 2028 to meet rising data archiving demand driven by generative AI [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
items.summary:
Fujifilm announced a $63 million investment to expand its Kanagawa Factory's capacity for producing LTO Ultrium10 magnetic tape, aiming to quintuple output by fiscal year 2028. The company attributes the surge in tape demand to exponential data growth from generative AI and highlights tape's cost-effectiveness and offline security benefits for large-scale data backup.

Magnetic tape remains widely used by cloud service providers and data centers for archiving due to its low cost and ability to air-gap data, providing protection against cyber threats like ransomware. Fujifilm's investment marks its largest dedicated expansion in tape manufacturing, reflecting continued enterprise reliance on tape storage despite consumer shifts away from the medium.

items.title: Nexus Mods requires AI usage disclosures for new mod uploads, mandates explanations for AI-assisted mods, and plans controls to manage AI content visibility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
items.summary:
Nexus Mods, the largest PC gaming mod repository, announced that mod authors must now disclose whether AI was used in their work when uploading new mods. The platform will require detailed explanations for AI-assisted mods and make AI-related tags more prominent to increase transparency. Nexus Mods will not ban AI-generated mods but aims to regulate and label them clearly to support pro-human creativity while acknowledging AI's role in the creation process.

The site also stated it will not use mods to train AI or license them for such purposes and is working on stronger attribution rules for mods that incorporate others' work. To address rapid mod production and prevent flooding, Nexus Mods will limit how many mods from a single author appear in the Recently Added section and impose stricter upload restrictions for new accounts. Additional controls to hide AI-generated content on game pages, the homepage, and search are planned. Mod authors have 60 days to update existing mods to comply with the new policy, with enforcement starting January 2nd.

items.title: PIMCO and Apollo warn of potential AI market downturn amid $2 trillion financing needs and rising bond issuances by tech giants [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
items.summary:
PIMCO's CEO Emmanuel Roman and Apollo Global Management's president Jim Zelter have expressed caution about the AI market, highlighting uncertainties in pricing and economics despite ongoing heavy investment. Major tech companies like Meta, Oracle, Alphabet, and Microsoft are issuing tens of billions in bonds to finance AI buildouts, contributing to an estimated $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years.

Roman noted that factors such as US interest rate hikes, geopolitical tensions, or a eurozone crisis could trigger a market downturn. While demand for AI-related bonds remains strong, with Meta's recent bond offering receiving $58 billion in orders, some signs of caution are emerging, including reports of an AI bubble burst in China and concerns following the Situational Awareness incident. The future trajectory of the AI market remains uncertain amid these mixed signals.

items.originalTitle: Should OpenAI Be Afraid of Jensen Huang?
items.summary:
Many Silicon Valley companies, including OpenAI, are cautious about challenging Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang due to his influence and control over AI chip supply critical for advanced model development. Nvidia's significant government connections and revenue from Chinese markets complicate the situation, as the company navigates restrictions on selling advanced chips directly to China.

OpenAI's reluctance to publicly address the debate over chip sales to China reflects its dependence on Nvidia's hardware and the desire to avoid jeopardizing access. Despite export controls, Chinese firms reportedly obtain Nvidia chips through indirect means, highlighting the complex dynamics between technology supply, geopolitics, and AI development.

items.originalSummary:
News flash: A lot of people in Silicon Valley are afraid of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

They have understandable reasons to be fearful, as Leo, Phoebe and I detailed in our story this morning. The chipmaker has a lot of money and influence to throw around, since Huang has the ear of several top government officials, including President Trump. 

More importantly for model developers like OpenAI, Nvidia controls the flow of AI chips they need to develop and run today’s most advanced models. It’s been hard enough for AI developers to get access to those chips, so it makes sense that the companies would want to avoid anything that might upset Huang.

This has led to a situation where OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the current debate over chip sales to China for fear of alienating Nvidia and Huang, which generates plenty of revenue from Chinese companies and wants access to the Chinese market itself. (Nvidia isn’t allowed to sell its most advanced tech directly to that market, but Chinese firms like ByteDance and DeepSeek still find a way to access the chips outside China’s borders or through smuggled hardware.)

items.summary:
Nvidia is reportedly leveraging its influence over customers and policymakers to shape chip export controls, particularly concerning China. This cautious approach contrasts with earlier, more vocal stances on export controls and reflects the complex dynamics between AI companies and chip manufacturers amid evolving US export regulations.

items.originalSummary:
Last month, OpenAI Senior Research Scientist Noam Brown posted a link in a company Slack channel to a news story about OpenAI’s changing stance on advanced chip sales to China and asked a blunt question: “What is our policy on chip exports?” OpenAI policy leaders responded on Slack by citing past company posts, such as a safety blueprint on frontier AI published in June, that supported general chip export controls but did not address China specifically. They also directed staffers to speak to members of the global affairs team working on new export control policies, rather than discussing it on Slack.

Chip restrictions are a delicate topic at the company. Over the past year, OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the issue of chip export controls for China because OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, have expressed concern that doing so will alienate chipmaker Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, according to people with knowledge of the company’s strategy. Last year, as Congress turned its attention to export control legislation, a senior OpenAI policy staffer privately said OpenAI was not as vocal on chip export controls as it had been under the Biden administration because it feared antagonizing Huang and Nvidia, according to a staffer on Capitol Hill.

items.title: Anthropic develops FlashProve, an open source system to cryptographically verify AI model outputs and confirm their origin [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.summary:
Anthropic is creating FlashProve, a system designed to provide cryptographic proof that a specific AI model produced a given output, allowing users to verify the model's identity. The system aims to prevent impersonation by impostor models and verify claims about AI-generated results without revealing proprietary model details.

FlashProve requires AI labs to publish a unique fingerprint for each model that can be matched to outputs and verified locally without exposing the model's internal weights. The project is open source, with technical specifications and code available on GitHub, but Anthropic has no immediate plans to deploy it internally, encouraging others to build on the research.

items.title: Google disables Search and AI features for K-12 schools that do not enable its AI tools, requiring administrators to activate them together [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google is entirely disabling Search in schools that don’t want AI
items.summary:
Google has announced that K-12 schools rejecting its AI features will have Google Search and AI-powered tools like Gemini and Gemini Notebook completely disabled for student accounts unless administrators explicitly enable them. The company stated that Search and AI are deeply integrated, so schools cannot disable AI features without losing Search access, and students will see a message indicating Search is unavailable if disabled.

This change follows Google's earlier decision to enable its Gemini AI assistant by default in Google Classroom, which serves over 150 million users globally. The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers and local officials who view it as coercive, while Google argues it provides schools with more control over AI feature usage. To address concerns about students using AI for shortcuts, Google plans to test a Guided Learning feature in select US schools to help students work through problems rather than bypassing learning.

items.title: AI Agenda Live: EY Consulting on Bringing AI ROI to your P&L [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Agenda Live: EY Consulting on Bringing AI ROI to your P&L
items.summary:
The capabilities AI can bring to companies seem limitless. So do AI token bills, which have skyrocketed, pressuring CFOs and boards to show that such spending can actually boost revenue or profits.

Dan Diasio, EY Global AI Leader and Consulting CTO, has led teams advising the world’s largest companies on their AI transformations. The Information Editor-in-Chief Jessica Lessin sat down with Diasio to discuss why productivity gains from AI aren’t automatically showing up as financial returns and what has to change for them to do so.

From enthusiasm to ROI

According to Diasio, rising token costs haven’t dampened enterprise enthusiasm for AI. But enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to move profit margins. To underscore this point, he referred to two surveys suggesting that many organizations believe AI is paying off, but few can yet trace those returns in their financial results. The first, conducted by The Information, found that a third of organizations reported getting a return from AI that was a multiple of what they spend on it. The second, an EY survey conducted as part of the EY CEO Imperative Series, found that only 11% of CEOs say their companies link AI impact to financial reporting and review it regularly at the senior management level.

“There’s value in increasing productivity, and there’s the value organizations need to be able to prove in their [profit and loss statement], and those are two different things,” Diasio said. “Many organizations I talk to would say AI is significantly increasing productivity. But when the CFO looks at the investment, that productivity needs to translate into two things: Are we making more revenue, and are we taking costs out of the organization?”

Thinking beyond use cases

What this means is that business leaders have to devise more concrete plans for AI than they did in past cycles.

“I’m seeing this big pivot from ‘let’s go identify some use cases’ to using AI to drive business transformation,” he said.

To illustrate the point, Diasio described how a consumer products company could use AI to cut the time from product idea to market from 18 months to three, a move that would drive revenue by bringing more products to market faster.

“That’s the sort of change that enterprises need to see to be all in,” he said.

The agent handoff

As part of that transformation, organizations are rethinking the relationship between human employees and so-called AI agents and, in many cases, finding unique ways to use agents to create value. Diasio pointed to banks, which have started using agents to assist financial advisors and streamline back-office work. The real value, he said, is in how those AI-assisted touch points build the bank’s relationships with clients and hopefully pay off by helping it generate more revenue.

“They’re using a lot of these AI capabilities not as a way of reducing costs, but of building brand,” he said of the banks.

Starting fresh

Ultimately, making AI’s payoff visible in financial results is going to require organizations to think of AI less as a technology rollout and more as a driver of measurable results. That means redesigning whole business functions from the ground up, not just automating pieces of them.

“Fast-forward 12 months and companies are going to start thinking about new ways to run their business in parts,” he said. “That means doing the hard thing: addressing the processes that need to be entirely rebuilt.”

That’s a harder path than simply adopting new tools, he said, but it’s the one that actually shows up on the P&L.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic Touts Claude’s Chip Design Skills to IPO Investors
items.summary:
Anthropic’s AI models have helped uncover serious cyber vulnerabilities and transform the software coding profession. Now the company is seeing just how much of an advantage its models can give it in unfamiliar terrain: designing its own AI chips.

The company, which is barreling toward an initial public offering later this month that could value it around $1.5 trillion, has told investors in recent meetings that its new 15-person chip design team is already using its own Claude models for engineering and design work on its custom chips, according to four people familiar with the discussions. Its engineers have found Claude cuts down the time it takes to design chips compared to their estimates of traditional workflows at large chip designers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, said some of the people.

items.originalTitle: AI Models Are Getting Harder to Monitor, Says U.K. Government’s Joseph Bloom
items.summary:
The ability to monitor AI models to detect what they’re trying to do and why is widely considered a crucial part of the effort to keep the technology operating safely. It’s also increasingly hard to do, said Joseph Bloom, the head of model transparency at the U.K. AI Security Institute.

“In general, we’re seeing monitorability—in various respects or from various angles—decrease,” Bloom said on the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive, in one of the first on-the-record interviews that a member of technical staff at AISI has given. (The full episode is available here.) The institute is one of the world’s largest government bodies focused on AI, and its work includes evaluating models from leading AI companies.

items.title: How Smugglers Get Expensive Memory Chips to China from South Korea [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How Smugglers Get Expensive Memory Chips to China from South Korea
items.summary:
For an illustration of how porous U.S. restrictions on the shipment of AI chips to China can be, consider a technique that has begun to catch on among smugglers involving a key type of memory chip.

While U.S. export regulations ban the shipment of high-bandwidth memory chips on their own to China, including from countries like South Korea, those rules have a loophole that allows the sales of those memory chips if they’re packaged together on plates with cheap server processors whose performance falls below the export restriction threshold. That’s because the computing power of the package gets determined by the server processor, not the memory chips, according to the rules.

The agent queries the database and filters millions of entries down to a handful of candidates worthy of attention.
